records.text: Douglas Blake Bednarz accuses Brian Harpole by name every day of murdering Charlie Kirk.

appearances.snippet: I did not yet turn the page when I thought he has to be talking about Douglas Blake Bednarz here because Douglas Blake Bednarz basically accuses by name Brian Harpole every single day of murdering Charlie Kirk.

records.text: A gun was never fired at Charlie Kirk; a pendant-shaped charge was detonated by Brian Harpole.
records.speaker: Douglas Blake Bednarz

appearances.snippet: His name is Brian Harpole from Dallas, Texas. Okay, third time. Douglas Blake Bednarz writes, a gun was never fired and a bullet did not hit his neck. The pendant shaped charge was detonated by Brian Harpole. This is why the necklace was such a central focus right after the incident.

verification.notes: The official FBI investigation describes Charlie Kirk as fatally shot from a rooftop, and Utah County formally charged Tyler Robinson in the shooting case. Those official records directly contradict the assertion that no gun was fired and that Brian Harpole detonated a pendant charge. Robinson is charged and is presumed innocent unless convicted; Harpole is not identified as the charged shooter in these records.

records.text: The item in Brian Harpole's front-right pants pocket caused audio interference, and he squeezed an item under his shirt when Charlie Kirk was hit.
records.speaker: Douglas Blake Bednarz

appearances.snippet: Here's another one. What did Brian Harpole have hidden on his person? Two things. One, the item in his front right pants pocket is what caused the audio interference. And the item under his shirt below his left armpit is what he squeezed discreetly at the moment that CK was hit. Holy smokes, But he squeezed discreetly at the moment that CK was hit.

verification.notes: The statement is Bednarz's interpretation of a small object and momentary audio interference in footage. Current official shooting materials do not identify the object or establish that it caused interference or concealed equipment; the visual inference cannot be conclusively verified from public evidence.

verification.notes: This is a behavioral interpretation of footage alleging Harpole repeatedly pulled his shirt to hide wires. Current official records do not identify concealed wires or a controller on Harpole, and the public footage alone does not establish intent.

records.text: Douglas Blake Bednarz received a preservation order from Dhillon Law Group rather than a lawsuit because Brian Harpole's side believed he might have information useful against Candace Owens.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: So you have to imagine my surprise. When I got contacted by Douglas Blake Bednarz himself, the man right there, and I learned that Douglas Blake Bednarz had been served by Dylan Law Group, but not with a lawsuit, with a simple preservation order because they think he might have something that might help to prosecute me in a defamation suit.

verification.notes: Bednarz publicly described receiving a preservation demand rather than being named as a defendant, and the current federal docket confirms that he is not a defendant in Harpole v. Owens. The explanation that counsel sought potentially useful evidence is consistent with the public account, although the underlying communication is not on the federal docket.

records.text: Douglas Blake Bednarz claimed to have never-before-seen footage from the Utah Valley University event but repeatedly failed to provide the promised long footage.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: And a girlfriend of mine contacted me and said, hey, there's this guy who is purporting to have never before seen footage from the UVU event. ... He just kind of never did that. He sent me a clip here, a clip there, a link to somebody else's footage. He just sort of kept kicking the can down the road. And eventually I just felt like something was off.

verification.notes: The claim combines Bednarz's asserted lack of prior access with a private promise to provide longer footage. The public interview preserves the competing account, but no authenticated message archive or delivery record establishes what was promised or previously viewed.
